terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; with animō or cōgitātiōne, or an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. N.D. 3.47: quae cōgitātiōne nōbīsmet ipsīs possumus fingere
terms.comment: The verb of shaping clay or wax, said of the mind: animō fingere, cōgitātiōne fingere. The same verb puts a case (see suppose) and makes believe (see pretend).

terms.gloss: picture, call up (literally, set before the eyes)
evidence: Cic. Phil. 2.115: pōne ante oculōs laetitiam senātūs

terms.comment: Post-Augustan (Quintilian, Pliny, Tacitus: Lewis & Short); Traupman’s word for “imagine” (p. 331).

phrases.latin: fingite animīs — līberae sunt enim nostrae cōgitātiōnēs et quae volunt sīc intuentur ut ea cernimus quae vidēmus
phrases.english: picture it in your minds — for our thoughts are free, and they see what they wish as plainly as we see what is before our eyes

phrases.latin: recordāre igitur illum, M. Antōnī, diem quō dictātūram sustulistī; pōne ante oculōs laetitiam senātūs populīque Rōmānī
phrases.english: remember, then, Mark Antony, the day on which you abolished the dictatorship; picture the joy of the senate and the Roman people

sources: Lewis & Short: fingo · Lewis & Short: pono · Lewis & Short: imaginor
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 331.
Cicero (Mil. 79, N.D. 3.47, Phil. 2.115) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
